Hard times

Infertility

A silent grief that affects one in six people: its emotional impact, myths about stress and what helps couples.

In 2023, the World Health Organization estimated that around one in six people of reproductive age experience infertility at some point in their lives, in rich and poor countries alike. Despite being so common, it is often lived in silence: each month brings hope and disappointment, and all around are pregnancies, intrusive questions and unwanted advice.

Distress comparable to serious illness

In a classic study, Alice Domar compared women with infertility with patients with cancer, heart disease and other chronic illnesses, and found similar levels of anxiety and depression. Infertility involves losses that are not always recognised: of the imagined child, of a sense of control over one's own body, of a life plan. It is a real grief, even without a funeral.

The "just relax and it will happen" myth

Many people are told they are not getting pregnant because they are anxious. A meta-analysis by Jacky Boivin of almost 3,600 women undergoing IVF found no link between prior emotional distress and the chance of pregnancy. Stress is a consequence of infertility, not its usual cause, and blaming the person adds pain. In addition, the emotional burden is the main reason many couples drop out of treatment early.

Each partner experiences it in their own way

It is common for one partner to want to talk about it constantly and the other to prefer not to, or for one to want to keep trying while the other needs to stop. It does not mean either cares less. It helps to set aside couple time that does not revolve around fertility and to agree limits together: how many attempts, how much money, when to rethink the path.

What tends to help

  • Clear information about chances and options, to decide with realistic expectations.
  • Specialist psychological support, which many fertility units offer and which reduces distress.
  • Choosing whom to tell and preparing a short answer for awkward questions.
  • Support groups with others going through the same.
  • Opening other doors when the time comes: adoption, fostering or a life without children can also be full lives.

References

  1. Organización Mundial de la Salud (2023). Infertility prevalence estimates, 1990–2021. Ginebra: OMS.
  2. Domar, A. D., Zuttermeister, P. C. y Friedman, R. (1993). The psychological impact of infertility: a comparison with patients with other medical conditions. Journal of Psychosomatic Obstetrics and Gynaecology, 14(Supl.), 45–52.
  3. Boivin, J., Griffiths, E. y Venetis, C. A. (2011). Emotional distress in infertile women and failure of assisted reproductive technologies: meta-analysis of prospective psychosocial studies. BMJ, 342, d223.
  4. Gameiro, S., Boivin, J., Peronace, L. y Verhaak, C. M. (2012). Why do patients discontinue fertility treatment? A systematic review of reasons and predictors of discontinuation. Human Reproduction Update, 18(6), 652–669.
